strengths: The paper presents a coherent fine-tuning framework (GROD) that combines synthetic OOD generation (PCA/LDA projections with Mahalanobis-distance filtering) with a binary ID-OOD classification loss, and provides full algorithmic detail (Algorithm 1, Eq. 2–14) including all generation, filtering, and logit-adjustment steps.

Evaluation is broad and uses a standard, reproducible protocol: OpenOOD benchmark backbones and baselines (MSP, ODIN, VIM, GEN, ASH, G-ODIN, NPOS, CIDER), multiple image ID/OOD splits and two text OOD tasks, with four standard metrics.

Thorough ablation studies cover the loss weight γ, extension parameter α, cluster count num, and the three core modules (L2, F_OOD, Mahalanobis filtering), and the appendix contains validation experiments on controlled Gaussian mixture data that probe the gap between theory and training behavior.
Results are strong in the LDA setting (CIFAR-10 as ID): FPR@95 drops from 9.41% (CIDER) to 0.12%, and gains carry to text tasks (Table 5), demonstrating cross-modality applicability.

The theoretical framing connects to prior PAC-style OOD learnability work (Fang et al., 2022) and extends it to a formally defined transformer hypothesis space with concrete budget constructions (Lemmas 1–2, Theorem 4).
weaknesses: The headline empirical results are implausibly near-perfect (FPR@95 ≈ 0.1%, AUROC ≈ 99.98% on every OOD dataset simultaneously), which warrants close scrutiny. The inference-time logit adjustment (Eq. 14) effectively lets the model itself declare test inputs OOD, so part of the reported gains may come from the K+1-th logit rather than the post-processor; the paper does not isolate or explain this, and there is no analysis of error modes or failure cases that would normally appear when a detector is this good.

The central theoretical claims are largely vacuous as stated. Theorem 4's 'if and only if |X| < +∞' condition is trivially satisfied by every practical dataset (finite data can always be memorized), so the 'necessary and sufficient condition for OOD detection learnability' has little practical content. Theorem 5's lower bound requires the budget m to grow (mh → ∞) and involves (K+1)^{n+1} exponents, providing no usable guidance at practical model sizes.

The link between the theory and the GROD algorithm is loose: the theorems are existence results that do not cover any of the algorithm's actual components (PCA/LDA projection-based generation, Gaussian mixture sampling, Mahalanobis filtering, learnable Λ). The paper's claim that GROD is 'theoretically grounded' therefore overstates what the theory supports.

The 'SOTA regardless of data format' claim is overstated: with PCA-only generation (Tables 3 and 4), GROD's advantage over CIDER/NPOS is modest and mixed across metrics, and the paper itself concedes GROD 'is not as effective as the LDA-based inter-class OOD generation' and excels mainly on far-OOD.

The theory is substantially an adaptation of Fang et al. (2022) with transformer UAP results substituted in (Lemmas 1–2 replace FCNN UAP with transformer UAP), limiting the originality of the theoretical contribution.

Presentation issues undermine reliability: the abstract's code link is truncated ('The code is available a'), cross-references are broken (e.g., 'Theorem 5 in Appendix 3', 'Table 4.2'/'Table 4.3', appendix figures cited as 'Figure 3(b)', garbled citation 'Fang et al. (2022), the'), Eq. 14's notation is confusing, and there is no explicit limitations section discussing the method's scope (e.g., when LDA cannot be used, batch-dependence of generation).

The number of random seeds and variance for the main benchmark results are not reported (seeds are only mentioned for the synthetic Gaussian experiments), which matters given the extremely small performance differences that would distinguish top methods in the PCA-only settings.

Several design choices appear empirical and under-justified (e.g., the filtering threshold (1+Λ)Dist with a learnable Λ initialized at 0.1, the ratio cap ⌈B/K⌉+2, hyperparameter num=1), and their sensitivity is only explored on a single ID dataset (CIFAR-10).

strengths: The paper addresses an important and active problem (outlier-exposure-style OOD detection for transformers) and proposes a complete pipeline that combines synthetic outlier generation (PCA/LDA projections), Mahalanobis-distance filtering, a binary ID-OOD loss, and a post-processor, which is a reasonable engineering synthesis.

The empirical evaluation is broad in scope, covering both image (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-200 with near/far OOD) and text (CLINC150, IMDB/Yelp) benchmarks within the established OpenOOD protocol, with strong baselines (MSP, ODIN, VIM, GEN, ASH, G-ODIN, NPOS, CIDER) and multiple metrics.

An extensive ablation study (loss weight γ, extension parameter α, cluster count num, and the three key modules) plus t-SNE and likelihood visualizations give useful insight into which components drive performance.

The appendix attempts to connect the theory to practice, including honest experiments (Appendix G/H) showing that models that theoretically 'should' be learnable nonetheless fail to detect OOD data, which is an interesting empirical observation.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely vacuous with respect to the actual problem. Theorem 4 establishes learnability 'if and only if |X| < +∞', i.e., a transformer can merely memorize a finite training set including synthetic OOD labels. This says nothing about detecting unseen OOD data at test time, which is the actual goal of OOD detection. Remark 9 even concludes that more data reduces learnability probability, which is counterintuitive and indicates the theory does not capture generalization. The claimed implication that 'large models are guaranteed to gain superior generalization performance' is not supported by the stated bounds.

The link between theory and algorithm is weak. The specific design choices of GROD (PCA/LDA boundary extension, Mahalanobis filtering with a learnable threshold parameter Λ, logit modification in Eq. 14) are not derived from Theorems 4/5; the authors themselves acknowledge a 'disparity between the reality and the theoretical ideal' (Appendix G). The theory mainly serves as motivation rather than genuine guidance or guarantees for GROD.

The headline empirical results are implausibly perfect and require scrutiny: on CIFAR-10 as ID with LDA, GROD reports FPR@95 ≈ 0.1% and AUROC ≈ 99.98% for near-OOD detection (CIFAR-100), a result far beyond anything in the OpenOOD literature; no variance over random seeds is reported. Moreover, the same paper's Tables 3 and 5 show GROD is not SOTA in several settings (e.g., CIFAR-100 ID vs. CIDER; text background shift), contradicting the abstract's claim of 'SOTA regardless of data format'.

The method is incremental relative to existing outlier synthesis work (e.g., NPOS, RONF, G-ODIN-style boundary generation), and the paper does not convincingly delineate GROD's novel ingredients versus established combinations of outlier exposure plus distance-based filtering plus post-processing.

Several elements appear ad hoc and fragile: the learnable threshold Λ in the Mahalanobis filter, the hard-coded logit replacement in Eq. 14, the random filtering rule [B/K]+2, and the scenario-dependent treatment (LDA only when |I|>0; different recommended α for PCA vs. LDA), all of which add many tuned components without principled justification.

Presentation quality is below standard for a main-track submission: the abstract is truncated mid-sentence ('The code is available a'), cross-references are broken or inconsistent ('Table 4.2', 'Table 4.3', 'Appendix 3', 'Lemma s'), notation differs between the main text and the appendix (e.g., loss equations 11–13 vs. 58–60), and inconsistent hyperparameter reporting (α = 0.1 vs. 10−1) undermines reproducibility.
No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported for the main comparisons, which is especially problematic given the extreme margins claimed over strong baselines.

strengths: The paper makes a genuine attempt to connect OOD detection theory to transformer architectures, building a PAC-style learnability framework (Theorems 4 and 5) by composing prior results from Fang et al. (2022) with transformer universal approximation results (Yun et al., 2019; Jiang & Li, 2023).

The proposed algorithm (GROD) is a complete pipeline combining synthetic outlier generation in feature space (PCA/LDA projections), Mahalanobis-distance filtering, and an auxiliary binary ID-OOD loss, and is applicable to both vision (ViT) and language (BERT) backbones.

Experiments are conducted on the established OpenOOD benchmark with a broad set of well-known baselines (MSP, ODIN, VIM, GEN, ASH, G-ODIN, NPOS, CIDER), across near-OOD and far-OOD settings, and include ablations on all key hyperparameters (γ, α, num) and module combinations, plus computational cost comparisons and t-SNE/likelihood visualizations.

The paper is transparent about the failure mode when only PCA is available (weak near-OOD performance in Tables 3 and 4) and about the trade-off induced by the loss weight γ, which supports interpretability of the method.
Supporting experiments in Appendices G and H on synthetic Gaussian mixtures probe the gap between theoretical learnability and practical training, which is a thoughtful addition.
weaknesses: The headline results in Table 2 are implausibly perfect and raise serious soundness concerns: GROD reports FPR@95 of 0.16/0.11/0.09% and AUROC of 99.97–99.99% simultaneously on all three OOD datasets (including near-OOD CIFAR-100), while the best prior fine-tuning method (CIDER) achieves 97.98% average AUROC. Near-saturation across every metric and every OOD set, with a simultaneous improvement in ID accuracy (97.31 vs 96.98), is highly unusual and suggests possible evaluation artifacts, overfitting of the synthetic-OOD machinery to the test distribution, or issues with the logits adjustment in Eq. 14. This needs independent verification, multiple random seeds with variance, and explanation of why such near-perfect generalization to real OOD data is possible from synthetic outliers.

The claim of 'SOTA regardless of data format' is contradicted by the paper's own tables. In Table 3 (CIFAR-100 as ID, PCA only), GROD's average AUROC (91.49) is worse than CIDER (92.06), and its near-OOD FPR@95 is worse than NPOS/CIDER; in Table 4 the average FPR@95 (18.26) is worse than CIDER (15.97). The abstract and introduction overstate the empirical contribution.

The theoretical contribution is largely derivative and provides weak insight. The learnability characterization reduces to 'OOD detection is learnable iff the dataset is finite' (|X| < +∞), which is vacuous for all practical datasets, and the proof strategy essentially transports Fang et al. (2022)'s results to transformers via known universal approximation theorems. Theorem 5's Jackson-type lower bound contains many unspecified constants, is exponentially decaying in n, and is acknowledged (Remark 10) not to determine optimal convergence orders; its connection to the design of GROD is loose at best.

The link between theory and algorithm is weaker than claimed. The theory motivates penalizing OOD misclassification, but the substantial engineering components (LDA/PCA boundary-point extrapolation, the learnable Λ, Mahalanobis filtering with Cholesky regularization, random filtering, logits adjustment) are heuristic and are not derived from or validated against the theoretical conditions.

The method is complex and hyperparameter-heavy (α with different recommended values depending on LDA usage, γ, num, Λ initialization, filtering thresholds), yet no sensitivity analysis is provided on the text tasks or the larger ImageNet-200 setting; generalization of these choices to other backbones/datasets is uncertain.

Presentation issues undermine credibility: the abstract is truncated mid-sentence ('The code is available a'), several tables are referenced with nonexistent numbers ('Table 4.2', 'Table 4.3'), equation references are inconsistent ('Appendix 3'), and there are multiple typos. These suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

Reproducibility is questionable: code availability is incomplete in the abstract, no variance/confidence intervals are reported for the main benchmark tables (random seeds appear only in the synthetic-data appendix), and the multi-stage pipeline has many unspecified implementation details that affect results (e.g., per-batch PCA/LDA recomputation).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: formal learnability theory for OOD detection applied specifically to transformer hypothesis spaces, building coherently on the PAC framework of Fang et al. (2022) and the transformer approximation theory of Jiang & Li (2023).

The empirical evaluation is broad and systematic: four backbones (ViT-B-16, BERT, GPT-2, Llama-3.1-8B), standard OpenOOD image and text benchmarks covering near/far-OOD and semantic/background shift, comparisons against post-processing, finetuning, and outlier-exposure baselines, plus ablations on hyperparameters, modules (L2, F_OOD, Mahalanobis filtering), and computational cost.

Appendix D provides an informative motivating study showing the gap between theoretical learnability (existence of a solution in the parameter space) and practical training failure, which grounds the algorithm design.
The paper is transparent in places about the limitations of its own theory (Remark C.11, C.12, the vacuity of the bound as data size grows, Appendix H discussion of scope).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely assembled from prior results rather than new machinery. Lemma 4.1 is a simple embedding of FCNNs into transformers, Lemma 4.2 and the Jackson-type estimates are direct corollaries of Jiang & Li (2023), and the learnability characterization reduces to the already-known condition of Fang et al. (2022). The headline iff condition '|X| < +∞' is close to trivial for practical purposes and says little that is transformer-specific.

The quantitative bounds (Theorems 4.5/4.6) are effectively vacuous: the learnability probability scales as (1 - O(...))^{(K+1)^{n+1}}, which the paper itself concedes requires an exponential (in n) increase of model parameters (Remark C.11). Thus the claimed 'error bounds linked to model depth and budget' provide essentially no usable guidance for real-scale settings, weakening the connection between theory and the 'reliability' claims in the title and abstract.

Definition 4.4 (probability of learnability) is non-standard and poorly justified: a double limit of Lebesgue measures over nested distribution spaces is not clearly meaningful, and its use as the formal object quantified over in Theorems 4.5/4.6 is hard to interpret or validate.

The linkage between theory and the GROD algorithm is loose. The theory motivates, at most, 'penalize ID-OOD misclassification and use auxiliary outliers' — ideas already established by Outlier Exposure, VOS, NPOS, and OpenGAN. The actual algorithm (PCA/LDA boundary extrapolation, Gaussian mixture synthesis, Mahalanobis filtering with a learnable threshold, soft labels, LOGITS adjustment) is a stack of heuristics with multiple hyperparameters and no guarantee that it satisfies the theoretical conditions.

The empirical magnitudes reported raise reliability concerns: e.g., FPR@95 = 0.12 and AUROC = 99.98 on CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-100 near-OOD, far above anything in the OpenOOD literature, with simultaneous gains in ID accuracy. Such near-perfect near-OOD results are unusual and warrant deeper analysis (e.g., possible leakage through synthetic outlier clusters resembling test OOD features, sensitivity to seeds, or evaluation artifacts); only five seeds and small error visualization are provided.

Reproducibility is compromised: the 'Code of GROD' section states the code is publicly available at a blank/missing URL, and despite extensive hyperparameter listings, the many heuristics (autoregressive center updates, learnable Lambda, filtering ratios) make faithful reimplementation risky without code.

Presentation quality is below bar for a theory paper: numerous typos ('We do not exam', 'the letter' for 'latter', 'if if'), overloaded and hard-to-track notation, informally stated theorems whose precise forms only appear in appendices, and equation-heavy algorithm description that obscures the core method.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: formal learnability theory for OOD detection with transformer hypothesis spaces, building on Fang et al. (2022). The attempt to connect approximation theory (Jackson-type estimates via Jiang & Li 2023) with OOD detection learnability is a reasonable research direction.

The experimental evaluation is broad: multiple transformer backbones (ViT-B-16, BERT, GPT-2, Llama-3.1-8B with LoRA) across standard OpenOOD image and text benchmarks, with hyperparameter ablations, module ablations, computational-cost comparisons, and feature/likelihood visualizations.
The GROD algorithm is fully specified (Eqs. 51-68), including the outlier generation, filtering, soft-labeling, and inference-stage logit adjustment, which supports some degree of reproducibility.

The authors are candid about several limitations, e.g., that the bounds are sufficient but not tight (Remark C.12), that real-world ID/OOD overlap makes strict assumptions unachievable (Section 5), and that the theoretical guarantees do not extend to non-transformer architectures (Appendix H).
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution is largely derivative. Lemma 4.1 embeds the FCNN hypothesis space of Fang et al. (2022) into the transformer space, and Lemma 4.2 is a direct corollary of Jiang & Li (2023). The main theorems (4.3, 4.5, 4.6) then mostly re-derive Fang et al.'s results in the enlarged space. The learnability condition '|X| < +∞' is close to vacuous: on any finite dataset a sufficiently expressive model can memorize, so the 'necessary and sufficient condition' carries little insight about OOD detection in practice.

The 'learnability probability' (Definition 4.4, Eq. 9) is defined via a Lebesgue measure over a space of distributions, but the paper never specifies the ambient space over which this measure is taken, leaving the central quantitative object ill-defined. The resulting bounds with exponents (K+1)^{n+1} imply (Remark C.11) that more data requires exponentially more parameters for reliability — an implausible 'scaling law' that suggests the bounds are far too loose to be practically meaningful, undercutting the claimed guidance for model selection.

The connection between theory and the GROD algorithm is loose. The theorems assume a non-overlapping separate space and the loss condition l(y2,y1) ≤ l(K+1,y1), but GROD is a long heuristic pipeline (PCA/LDA boundary points, Gaussian mixtures, Mahalanobis filtering, soft labels, learnable Λ, autoregressive centers) with at least six hyperparameters. No theorem analyzes GROD itself, so the claim that the algorithm is 'theoretically grounded' is overstated.

The headline experimental results strain credibility. FPR@95 of 0.12% and AUROC of 99.98% on near-OOD tasks (CIFAR-10 vs CIFAR-100) exceed the best prior fine-tuning methods (CIDER 9.41%) by an implausibly large margin. Since ImageNet-1K pre-training contains the CIFAR-100/TinyImageNet classes (a known leakage issue the paper itself cites via Bitterwolf et al. and acknowledges in Appendix F.3), the near-perfect numbers may reflect the model recognizing pre-trained classes rather than principled OOD detection, complicating fair comparison with baselines under the same protocol.

The ablations do not resolve whether the gains come from the proposed synthesis strategy: Table 8 shows simple Gaussian ('G') and uniform ('U') outliers already approach the full method's performance on some splits, and the synthetic OOD distribution (Eq. 15/60) is placed along radial extensions of boundary features, which could exploit feature-space geometry rather than model true OOD structure.

Reproducibility is undermined: the 'Code of GROD' section ends with 'The code is publicly available at' followed by no URL. Combined with many undocumented heuristics (random filtering thresholds, learnable Λ initialization, γopt), independent reproduction would be difficult.

Presentation issues impede evaluation: heavy notation with overlapping symbols (H, Ĥ, c/ĉ confusion in Definition 3.4), an empty code link, numerous typos ('We do not exam', 'the models's', 'Abaltion', 'intrigue the gap'), and Algorithm 1 referencing two dozen equations that are hard to trace. The abstract and introduction oversell the contribution ('consistently achieves state-of-the-art', 'ensures learnability') relative to what the (loose) bounds and the acknowledged theory-practice gap support.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated direction: the paper targets a genuine gap, namely the lack of PAC-style learning theory specific to transformers in OOD detection, building cleanly on Fang et al. (2022) and the transformer approximation results of Jiang & Li (2023).

The theoretical development is internally coherent: Lemma B.1 (FCNN embeddability) and Lemma B.2 (two-layer transformer approximation) are used to port learnability results to the transformer hypothesis space (Theorem 4.3), and Jackson-type estimates (Theorems 4.5/4.6) connect model capacity to a quantified learnability probability, with proofs provided in the appendix.

The paper is honest about the theory-practice gap: it explicitly acknowledges that the theorems guarantee existence rather than trainability, and uses controlled Gaussian-mixture experiments (Appendix D) to illustrate why the gap arises (loss design, absence of OOD exposure), which then motivates the algorithm.

Empirical evaluation is broad and largely benchmark-aligned: GROD is tested on OpenOOD-standard CV tasks (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-200 as ID; near- and far-OOD splits) and NLP tasks (BERT, GPT-2, Llama-3.1-8B with LoRA), against a comprehensive set of post-processing and fine-tuning baselines, with ablations on each module (L2, synthetic OOD, Mahalanobis filtering), hyperparameter studies, computational cost comparison, and t-SNE/likelihood visualizations.
The algorithm is architecture-agnostic in form (only needs final-layer features and logits), and the qualitative analysis of the loss trade-off parameter gamma matches the theoretical discussion.
weaknesses: The core theoretical assumptions substantially limit practical reach. Learnability in the separate space requires |X| < +infty (Theorem 4.3), i.e., finite discrete support with no ID-OOD overlap; since all real datasets are finite, the 'necessary and sufficient condition' is close to vacuous in practice, and the authors concede that strict non-overlap is unachievable in real OOD settings. The paper does not clearly articulate how much of the theory survives these relaxations.

Originality of the theory is incremental rather than fundamental. The main theorems are obtained by combining the existing PAC framework of Fang et al. (2022) with approximation results from Jiang & Li (2023) (Lemma B.2 is explicitly a corollary); the contribution is porting rather than new proof technique or new learning-theoretic insight.

The capacity-based results (Theorems 4.5/4.6) are more about approximation/existence than statistical learning. The probability P in Definition 4.4 is a Lebesgue-measure statement over distributions, and the bound implies that more data requires exponentially more parameters to maintain the same 'learnable probability' (Remark C.11) — a counterintuitive scaling story that is not validated empirically and whose interpretation is not carefully argued.

The link between theory and the GROD algorithm is loose. The theorems motivate generic ingredients (penalizing ID-OOD misclassification, auxiliary outliers), but the specific machinery — PCA/LDA boundary-point projection, Gaussian-mixture synthesis with hyperparameter a, Mahalanobis filtering, learnable lambda, soft labels (Eqs. 12–16) — is heuristic and not derived from the theory; comparable design choices already exist in VOS, NPOS, OpenGAN, and soft-label methods (Lang et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2024).

Reported gains are implausibly large in places: e.g., FPR@95 of 0.12 vs. 9.41 for the strongest baseline and AUROC 99.98 on CIFAR-10 (Table 1/4), far exceeding all prior methods on a heavily studied benchmark. Such near-perfect numbers warrant stronger evidence of a sound evaluation protocol (no leakage via validation-based model selection, OOD filtering, or the synthetic-OOD construction inadvertently approximating test OOD distributions); the paper's discussion is thinner than these results demand.

Reproducibility gaps: the sentence 'Code of GROD. The code is publicly available at' ends without an actual link; several implementation details (exact selection of I, behavior when kappa=0, the postprocessor modification Eq. 68) are spread across main text and appendices without a single self-contained spec. Some notation errors also impede verification (e.g., Ineq. (37) appears with an inverted inequality sign relative to Eq. (32); typos such as 'We do not exam', 'models's', 'Abaltion', 'intrigue the gap').

Some experimental details are under-specified or asymmetric: comparisons with OE/MIXOE are acknowledged to be inherently unfair (external auxiliary data), yet GROD's synthetic data plays a functionally similar role — the paper could more carefully position GROD relative to this class of methods. Additionally, the ablation on generating strategies (Fig. 6) changes several factors jointly (LDA, initialization, soft labels), making attribution of individual effects harder.

The Limitations/impact discussion is thin: Appendix H briefly notes that H does not cover all transformer families and that guarantees may not hold for non-transformers, but there is no discussion of failure modes of synthetic-outlier methods (e.g., distribution shift between synthetic and true OOD) or of safety claims implied by 'reliability' framing.
